# The Rental Market {#sec-market-rental} ## Who rents ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Warrenton is the county's clearest concentration of renters](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-renter-share-1.png){#fig-renter-share fig-align='left' fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart of the renter share of occupied households in 2024 for Warrenton, Fauquier County, Bealeton, and Virginia. Warrenton is about 37% renter, well above Fauquier County and Bealeton at roughly 21% each; Virginia sits at about 33%. Renter household counts are labeled on each bar.' width=100%} ::: ::: Fauquier is overwhelmingly an ownership county: only about 21% of households rent. For context, 33% of Virginia's households are renters. Folks come to Fauquier to buy, and there is a limited rental market. Warrenton is the exception: roughly 37% of the town's 3,985 households rent, nearly double the county rate. Warrenton represents the county's principal rental submarket. Bealeton, on the other hand, tracks with the county at about 21% of its households renting. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Reliability Bealeton's renter count is small and carries Medium reliability, so it is read as a count, not a precise rate. ::: ## What renters pay ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Every measure of rent has climbed, and broker-placed leases run highest](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-rent-trend-1.png){#fig-rent-trend fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of Fauquier County rents in current dollars. The ACS median gross rent rises from about $1,138 in 2013 to $1,613 in 2024. CoStar asking rents, quarterly from 2016, climb at market-rate apartments to about $1,777 and at affordable (rent-restricted or subsidized) apartments to about $1,529. The MLS median closed lease, mostly single-family homes and townhouses, runs highest, rising from $1,950 in 2022 to $2,500 in 2026 to date. Town points for Warrenton and Bealeton sit near the county ACS line.' width=100%} ::: ::: The county's median gross rent, meaning all housing costs including lease rent and utilities, rose from $1,138 in 2013 to $1,613 in 2024, an increase of 42%. Over the same years, prices for everyday goods and services other than housing rose about 27%, so rents have outpaced general inflation and renters have lost ground. The other rent measures tell the same story at different price points. CoStar asking rents at the county's market-rate apartments reached about $1,777 in 2026 Q3, above the ACS median, while the larger set of affordable (rent-restricted or subsidized) apartments asked about $1,529. The MLS median closed lease kept rising after the ACS series ends, from $1,950 in 2022 to $2,500 in 2026 to date; these broker-placed leases skew toward single-family homes and townhouses and price well above the other measures. This report uses the ACS median gross rent as its affordability benchmark (@sec-gaps), since it covers the full rental universe, while CoStar tracks only professionally managed apartment communities. ::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"} In spring 2026, an interviewee shared that "Only about 2 of 19 available rentals were priced under $1,700." ::: Town rents track the county: Warrenton and Bealeton median 2024 rent (High reliability) sits roughly within $50 to $200 of the county figure. ## Where the rental stock prices ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Most rentals now price at $1,500 or more](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-rent-distribution-1.png){#fig-rent-distribution fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of the gross rent distribution for cash-rent renters in Fauquier County, Warrenton, and Bealeton across six rent bands. The $1,500–$1,999 band is the largest in the county at roughly a quarter of renters, and shares rise sharply above $1,000; bands under $1,000 are thin. Town bars with too few sample cases are omitted.' width=100%} ::: ::: The modal rent band in the county is $1,500–1,999 and represents about 25% of county cash-rent renters. Combined with the bands above it, most renters now pay $1,500 or more. Under $1,000 monthly rentals are scarce, representing only about 14% of the county's renters, underscoring how little of the stock is affordable to lower-income households. ::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"} Realtors in particular recognized the challenges renters face, noting that the MLS median rent sits at $2,450: "It's an outrageously expensive market." Rental quality was a consistent topic as well, with interviewees reporting that quality is rarely reflected in the price. ::: In 2025, the MLS recorded that only 28 of 203 closed leases were under $1,700, about 14%. That share has shrunk quickly, from 35% of leases in 2022 to 10% in 2026 to date. These data identify a median county lease of $2,450 monthly, consistent with the Greater Piedmont REALTOR's March 2026 study. This leaves a somewhat larger affordable share than the single snapshot of available rentals suggested, but the story is the same: sub-$1,700 rentals are scarce, and most of the rental market prices well above that (@fig-rent-distribution, @fig-rent-trend). The MLS median runs well above the county's ACS median gross rent ($1,613) because MLS only captures leases placed through a broker, which skew toward larger single-family homes and townhouses (the bulk of this study's rental stock) rather than the smaller apartment units that lease in-house and never reach MLS. ::: {.callout-note} ## What is listed for rent now As of October 2026, the MLS shows **41 active rental listings** with a median asking rent of **$2,900**, well above the 2025 closed-lease median of $2,450 and the $2,500 median across 195 leases closed so far in 2026 (through October 2026). Only 3 listings (7.3%) ask under $1,700, fewer in share than the 2025 closed leases (14%). Asking rents run above closed leases and this is a small single-day snapshot, so read it as directional rather than as a market-wide rent. ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Data note: place-level distributions Place-level distributions are noisy; only the higher-count Warrenton bands survive the reliability screen, and they mirror the county's upward concentration. ::: ## The professional apartment market ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Apartment rents keep rising at market-rate and affordable properties](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-costar-1.png){#fig-costar fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of quarterly CoStar asking rent per unit in current dollars, Fauquier County, 2016 through 2026 Q3, split by property type. Market-rate apartments rise from about $1,321 to about $1,777; affordable (rent-restricted or subsidized) apartments rise from about $1,011 to about $1,529, dipping slightly in the latest quarter.' width=100%} ::: ::: The professional rental market is small. Roughly 41 multifamily properties appear in the broader CoStar inventory, and CoStar tracks quarterly rents at 14 apartment properties with about 998 units. Most of those units, about 808, are at affordable properties that are rent-restricted or subsidized; only about 190 are at market-rate properties. Asking rents at the market-rate properties averaged about $1,777 in 2026 Q3, up 34% since early 2016. Affordable properties asked about $1,529, up 51%. For comparison, prices for everyday goods and services other than housing rose about 29% from 2016 to 2025, so apartment rents of both kinds have outpaced general inflation. New supply is on the way. Summit at Bealeton, a 160-unit market-rate community in Bealeton, is under construction with asking rents near $2,326. That would nearly double the market-rate apartment units CoStar tracks, at rents well above the current market-rate average (@sec-inventory). ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Apartment vacancy has edged up, driven by affordable properties](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-costar-vacancy-1.png){#fig-costar-vacancy fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of quarterly CoStar vacancy rates, Fauquier County, 2016 through 2026 Q3. The overall rate falls from about 5% to near 1% around 2019–2021, then rises to about 4.0% in the latest quarter. Affordable properties drive the increase, reaching about 4.5%, while market-rate properties stay near 1.6%.' width=100%} ::: ::: Fauquier's professional rental market remains tight, though slack has crept in. Vacancy across the tracked apartments averaged about 3.5% over the last four quarters (4.0% in 2026 Q3), up from about 1.2% in 2019–2021. Even so, it has been under 3% in 58% of quarters since 2016. The increase sits at the affordable properties, where vacancy reached about 4.5% (3.8% a year earlier); market-rate vacancy is about 1.6%. Much of it comes from one property: The Aspens Apartments (238 units) reports 9% vacancy and 8.3% concessions in the latest quarter. ## Rental stock by structure type ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Most of Fauquier's rental stock is single-family homes, not apartments](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-rental-structure-1.png){#fig-rental-structure fig-align='left' fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart of Fauquier County\'s renter-occupied housing units by structure type. Single-family detached homes are the largest share at about 57% of rentals, followed by 20-plus-unit buildings and 5-to-19-unit buildings; single-family detached and attached together make up roughly two-thirds of the rental stock.' width=100%} ::: ::: Single-family homes are the backbone of the county's rental market, about 68% of all renter-occupied units (attached and detached). Single-family detached alone is roughly 57% of the rental market. Purpose-built apartments (5+ units) are only about 20% of rentals, the mirror image of @fig-costar's thin professional market. This could be why so much of the rental supply behaves like the for-sale market: the reliance on scattered single-family rentals means renters compete for the same limited housing stock as buyers.[^rental-structure] [^rental-structure]: Place-level structure detail is too small to size reliably, so this is shown county-wide. ## Fair Market Rents vs. actual rents ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Metro Fair Market Rents run well above what Fauquier renters actually pay](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-fmr-1.png){#fig-fmr fig-align='left' fig-alt='Dot-and-range chart comparing rents by bedroom size in Fauquier County. For one- through four-bedroom units, the HUD metro-area Fair Market Rent sits far above the ACS actual median gross rent; the Small Area FMR range across the three town ZIP codes falls between the two but still above the local median. The gap is largest for one- and two-bedroom units.' width=100%} ::: ::: Because Fauquier is folded into the high-cost Washington, D.C. metro FMR area, the county's two bedroom (2BR) FMR at $2,246 sits far above the actual ACS median 2BR rent of $1,437. This is a gap of roughly $800. Small Area FMRs (SAFMRs) pull the benchmark towards what locals actually experience, described as a high cost and scarce rental environment. SAFMRs still land above the ACS median rent at every bedroom size, with the Warrenton and Bealeton 2BR SAFMR ranges from $1,520 to $2,340, with Bealeton (22712) at the lowest. The practical implication in the differences in FMR and ACS rents is ultimately favorable for voucher holders, with generous payment standards. However, this means FMRs overstate the going asking rental market and can be a poor gauge of local affordability. The ACS medians (@fig-rent-trend) are the better yardstick for rooting rents into local reality. ::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"} An interviewee noted that metro-based Fair Market Rents give voucher holders generous payment standards relative to what local rents actually are. ::: ## Assisted inventory & preservation risk ::: {#tbl-nhpd .cell layout-align="left" tbl-cap='Federally assisted rental properties, sorted by earliest subsidy expiration'} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: Fauquier's assisted housing rental stock consists of 874 units across 13 federally supported properties. This is a small cushion against the market rents documented above. The program mix locally is dominated by Low-Income Housing Tax Credit deals, with a handful of older project-based Section 8, PRAC/811 (elderly/disabled project rental assistance), and USDA Rural Housing (515) properties whose subsidies are the closest to expiring. Rental affordability preservation at these properties is a real risk and near-term, with the soonest subsidy expiration in January 2027. Additionally, 8 of the 13 properties have a subsidy expiring by 2036, the window in which preservation decisions must be made. As assistance units are aging, the quality of these rentals throughout the county is likely lower comparatively to the other aging single family rentals. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Town spotlight — assisted units concentrate in and around Warrenton **Most of the county's assisted properties sit in Warrenton** (6 of 13, about 475 units), the same submarket that carries the county's highest renter share (@fig-renter-share). **Bealeton has a smaller assisted base** of 3 properties and about 196 units, including the Mintbrook senior apartments. Beyond those, affordable options in Bealeton depend on scattered single-family and market-rate units that price low, which @fig-rent-distribution **shows is a shrinking share**. The 160-unit Summit at Bealeton will add market-rate apartments to the town, asking about $2,326 a month. :::
